Chatbots cite fake shops

12 November 2026 · Reading time: 6 minutes · Audio in the app: 8 minutes. Listening to the briefing is part of Sapaude Pro.

ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity showed shoppers risky websites in 9 percent of 6,795 answers, according to a test by the IP protection firm Podqi that The Verge reported on 12 November.

Sapaude retells the story in its own words. The source is below. Publisher: Sapaude.

In three points

Three points, in this order: what the source shows, where that claim stops, and what to check next.

  1. Podqi put five where-to-buy questions about 151 brands to the three chatbots in two waves in September, with data from the AI search firm Gauge. Perplexity showed a risky site in 15 percent of its answers, ChatGPT in 8 percent, Gemini in 4 percent.
  2. When a risky site appeared, the answer recommended it 57 percent of the time and warned against it 9 percent of the time. Podqi wrote the prompts itself, counts dead domains as risky and sells brand protection. Madhappy, one of the 151 brands, is a client.
  3. Podqi's CEO told The Verge to verify the source before entering personal or card details. Podqi's advice: treat any AI-supplied regional or official URL as unverified and reach country stores through the brand's main site.

Risky sites in nine percent of answers

Shoppers who ask a chatbot where to buy something are now handed a store name inside the answer, not a page of links to weigh themselves. A study by the IP protection firm Podqi, shared exclusively with The Verge and published on 12 November 2026, tried to measure how often that goes wrong. The Verge notes the timing: the holiday shopping season is coming, when people hunt for in-stock items and the best prices, and more of them will shop through AI, including at sites they do not know.

Podqi asked ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity the same five shopping questions about 151 brands, on the same days, in two waves of fieldwork in September. The brands included Lululemon, Birkenstock, Stüssy, Le Creuset and Madhappy, which is a Podqi client. Data collection ran with the AI search company Gauge, on the logged-out consumer versions of the three chatbots. Podqi analyzed 6,795 answers, 2,265 per chatbot, reviewed 4,437 domains and flagged 718 as risky.

A site counted as risky if it appeared to impersonate a brand or sell counterfeits, if it was an old brand domain that someone else had registered again, or if it was dead, meaning nothing a shopper could buy. Overall, 9 percent of answers showed a risky site: 15 percent for Perplexity, 8 percent for ChatGPT, 4 percent for Gemini. Of the 718 domains, 351 were fake and 367 dead.

Shipping questions were the riskiest

The five questions asked for the top websites for a brand, for products like it, for where to find it online, for where else to buy it besides its own site, and whether it ships internationally, with its regional websites. That last one was the riskiest, with 16 percent of answers showing a risky site. The top-websites question came to 11 percent, the other three to 6 or 7 percent. Each question drew 1,359 answers.

When an answer showed a risky site, it recommended it as a place to buy in 57 percent of cases, mentioned it without comment in 34 percent and warned the shopper away in 9 percent. Recommendations outnumbered warnings 6.3 to 1. Answers that mixed advice and caution counted as not warned. ChatGPT warned in 24 percent of its risky answers, the best rate of the three. Podqi says about one in five mishandled answers warned about counterfeits in general, which it does not count as protection: a warning helps only if it names the site the shopper is about to open.

The Verge singles out one case. Perplexity named the wrong page as Stüssy's official website and called it "the best starting point for guaranteed authentic items." The engines also at times listed regional sites for brands that have none, and 36 percent of the risky sites in regional answers used a country ending or a region name. Smaller brands were more exposed: answers about larger companies showed a risky site about half as often. Podqi adds that 4 of 125 risky answers about enterprise brands warned the shopper.

Written prompts, and a vendor's interest

Podqi crafted its own prompts instead of using real user conversations, and tracked the answers with a tool that follows AI answers across chatbots. The rates describe these five questions and these 151 brands in September. They do not describe what chatbots tell people in general.

Podqi also sells the remedy. It finds lookalike sites and files takedowns, and one of the 151 brands is its client. Between the two waves, risk fell from 12 to 7 percent, which Podqi reads as a sign that the problem is fixable. A side count of Google AI Overviews found 7 risky answers, all with a warning, too few to set beside the other three.

The companies answered The Verge. Google said it was happy to see Gemini perform best, that Gemini can make mistakes and that it shows source links so people can check. OpenAI said it keeps improving safeguards so that deceptive sites are less likely to appear in shopping results. Perplexity said it is consistently the most accurate AI on credible research benchmarks and has been for four years, and that it never claims to be 100 percent accurate.

Check the domain before you pay

Podqi's CEO and cofounder Trevor West told The Verge that consumers should know that, even when a chatbot hands them a result, it is best to verify the source before entering personal or credit card information. In the study's own words, today's dead domains are tomorrow's fakes: anyone can register a lapsed domain, so an address that AI keeps recommending could turn into a counterfeit store.

In practice that means opening the brand's own website, the one you already trust, and finding the country store there instead of following the link from the answer. If the domains differ, treat the chatbot's address as unverified and keep card number, password and delivery address out of it.

For brands, Podqi suggests one crawlable page that lists every official regional store and says which countries have none, plus a watch on country-code domains the brand does and does not own. The study does not test whether chatbots would copy such a page.

What you can do

Before you pay on a shop a chatbot named, open the brand's own site and compare the domain. If you only know the shop from an AI answer, keep your card details out of it.
